title: Neutral atom quantum computing for materials science and quantum chemistry
abstract: Neutral atom arrays have emerged as versatile platforms for performing both digital and analogue quantum computing and simulation, with demonstrations ranging from large-scale programmable Hamiltonians realising topological phases or weighted graph optimisation to error-corrected logical qubits with transverse gate operations. This paper provides a broad overview to the neutral atom platform, and the potential applications relevant to materials science and quantum chemistry.
summary: This paper reviews neutral atom arrays as a powerful, scalable platform for quantum simulation and computation. It details how the system can model complex Hamiltonians relevant to materials science and quantum chemistry using techniques like adiabatic state preparation and Rydberg blockade. The work demonstrates the platform's versatility for both simulating quantum phases and solving hard optimization problems.
main_problem: The primary goal is simulating complex quantum systems relevant to materials science and quantum chemistry, which involves determining ground state configurations or modeling dynamic evolution.
main_result: Neutral atom arrays are shown to be a highly scalable and versatile platform capable of realizing programmable Hamiltonians for both digital and analogue quantum simulation.
method: The paper details using adiabatic ramping of detuning to prepare the system in the ground state, alongside utilizing the Rydberg blockade for controlled gate operations.
model_or_system: The physical system is neutral atom arrays trapped in optical tweezers. The dynamics are modeled using Hamiltonians like the Ising Hamiltonian, governed by dipole-dipole coupling $V(r) \propto 1/r^6$.
key_observables: Z2-ordered crystalline states, correlation functions (for phase characterization), and the final ground state mapping to solutions of graph problems like MWIS.
important_parameters: Gate fidelities ($F \gtrsim 99.5\%$), blockade radius ($r_b$), and the ability to scale to thousands of qubits.
main_assumptions: Initial loading of atoms is stochastic, and achieving defect-free arrays requires advanced real-time rearrangement techniques.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup using optical tweezers, the preparation of Z2-ordered crystalline states in 1D and 2D lattices, and the general process flow for mapping graph optimization problems onto the atomic array.
paper_structure: The paper provides a broad overview, first detailing the platform's capabilities for quantum simulation (analogue approach) and then covering its use for digital computation and solving hard classical optimization problems.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it bridges fundamental AMO physics (Rydberg interactions, cold atom control) directly to cutting-edge quantum simulation and computation for chemistry and materials science.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) Schematic of a neutral atom quantum computer. Atom arrays are formed using arrays of microscopic optical tweezers created using reconﬁgurable holograms on a spatial light modulator (SLM) with atom sorting achieved using a fast mobile tweezer created using a crossed acousto-optical deﬂector (AOD) which can be combined on a polarising beam splitter (PBS). A high numerical-aperture objective lens is used to focus the tweezers and collect single atom ﬂuorescence onto a camera for atom readout, using dichroic mirror to separate the wavelengths (DM). (b) An example image of atoms trapped in a 15×15 array using the experimental platform from [82].

FIG. 2. Quantum simulation on a neutral atom array (a) A 1-D chain of atoms spaced with a < rb can be prepared in the Z2-ordered phase with every other site Rydberg excited using adiabatic control of the global drive parameters Ω(t),∆(t) (b) Experimental data showing adiabatic evolution for a chain of 7 atoms towards the Z2 ordered state adapted from [67]. (c) Extending to 2D geometries provides access to phase-diagrams on square lattices [58, 59] (d) Placing atoms on the edges of a kagome lattice enables mapping to a dimer model on which it has been possible to prepare topological quantum spin liquids on a neutral atom array [60].

FIG. 3. Graph optimisation on neutral atom arrays. Starting from an initial graph problem (a), the ﬁrst step is to embed the problem graph on a unit-disk (UD) graph as shown in (b) such that connected vertices are represented by atoms spaced within a blockade radius. FIG. 4. (a) Zonal architecture use for scalable digital quantum computation introduced by [50, 52]. The array ﬁeld of view is divided into four zones - a storage zone for data qubits, a gate zone in which atom pairs placed close together undergo high-ﬁdelity two-qubit gate operations, a readout zone enabling local detection and mid-circuit readout and a reservoir zone for replacing atoms lost during computation.
